items.rubric_text: The game opens to a title over a dried-up farm, the drought scene can be watched or skipped, and the player picks a village from the main menu.
items.comment: The game opens on a 3D camera sweep over a sun-baked village-1 farm with the WELLSPRING title and three drought captions, and it can be watched (auto-advances after 15s) or skipped. The main menu has Start/How to Play/Settings and a 12-card village selector.

items.rubric_text: The village loads from a top-down view with the spring gushing and the fields waiting at the far end, and the hunger meter is already running.
items.comment: Villages load in an angled top-down view with the spring basin bubbling behind its gate at the top and the field plots at the bottom edge. The hunger meter starts draining on load, before any input (134s down to 131s while idle).

items.rubric_text: The player can at least dig channels, raise walls, move stones, and open blocked paths to redirect the spring water.
items.comment: Left-drag digs channels, Shift+drag raises walls, right-click picks up and drops stones, and clicking rubble walls or sluice gates clears or opens them. Digging, walls and stones were driven with real mouse input, and gate/wall clicks were checked in code and simulation.

items.rubric_text: The player opens the spring, and the water spills out and follows the terrain the player shaped.
items.comment: Clicking the spring gate (or the Open Spring button) releases the water. It runs down the channel the player carved through the ridge and spills along low ground elsewhere.
items.claude_reason: Clicking the spring gate (or the Open Spring button) releases the water. It runs down the channel the player carved through the ridge and spills along low ground elsewhere.

items.rubric_text: The player fixes leaks and traps as the water runs, steering it without losing too much water to the dry ground.
items.comment: Tools stay usable while the water runs, and cracks, sand, open pits, faults, dry ground and map edges all drain water into a lost-water total that can fail the level. Many villages were solved by routing before opening the spring, so live steering is possible but rarely forced.

items.rubric_text: The water reaches the fields, the crops drink, and the village is saved before the hunger meter empties.
items.comment: Once water reaches a field along a connected wet path, the field fills, its crops turn green and the badge reads WATERED. The village is saved with hunger time to spare.
items.claude_reason: Once water reaches a field along a connected wet path, the field fills, its crops turn green and the badge reads WATERED. The village is saved with hunger time to spare.

items.rubric_text: The saved village turns green, and the player is carried to the next village down the valley, which is larger and harder.
items.comment: A saved village greens over for about 2 seconds, then a VILLAGE SAVED screen with a valley map leads to the next village. Grids and field counts grow (24x26/1 field up to 36x36/4 fields), but villages 2-4 save themselves when the spring is simply opened, so 'harder' does not hold at every step.

items.rubric_text: If the hunger meter empties first the village fails and can be retried, and if the last village is saved the ending scene plays and the watershed turns green.
items.comment: When hunger empties, a 'Drought Prevails' screen offers Retry and Back to menu, and Retry reloads the village. Saving village 12 plays 'The Watershed Restored' ending, where a green wave sweeps the delta under a blue sky.

items.rubric_text: Water leaves the spring and follows the terrain downhill, changes course wherever the player has dug a channel or lifted the land, and reaches the field only when an unbroken downhill path connects spring to field.
items.comment: Water is a real heightfield simulation: it flows to lower neighbours, follows dug channels, is blocked by walls, and fields drink only from cells reached by a breadth-first search from the spring. The 'unbroken path' check is lenient: a cell that was once wet keeps counting as connected because wetness never decays.

items.rubric_text: The player can at least dig channels and raise walls on soft ground but not on rock faces, with each shape staying until it is reworked, and can pick up and drop small stones to dam or deflect water while boulders roll downhill on steep slopes, crushing anything in the way, and can only be nudged slowly.
items.comment: It's possible to pick the rocks, but the controls don't work properly on that
items.claude_reason: Digging and walls are refused on granite (shovelAt returned false), and shapes persist. Stones can be picked up and dropped, boulders roll and crush channels once the slope is steep enough (digging below one sent it 7 cells down and erased the channel), and right-click nudges a boulder about 1 cell. One deviation: a single left-click deletes a boulder outright, which undercuts 'only nudged slowly'.

items.rubric_text: The ground holds at least cracks, holes, and thirsty sand that swallow water, and hidden pits that open under the water's weight; the hunger meter drains from the moment the village loads and the level is lost when it empties; a village is saved when enough water reaches each of its fields, which drink only the water that arrives while the path is whole; and wasted water is water the fields never get, so losing too much of it forces a restart.
items.comment: The ground holds cracks, open pits, thirsty sand, hidden pits that collapse after enough water weight, and fault seams. Hunger drains from load and fails the level at zero, fields drink only connected arriving water, and running out of supply below the remaining need triggers a water-loss fail (seen in sims at ~29s).

items.rubric_text: The first village is a single straight downhill channel with one field so the player learns to dig before anything else exists, each later mechanic is introduced on a village where it is the only new thing, and the player can only lose by running out of time, never by a mechanic they have not met.
items.comment: Village 1 is a single straight pre-cut channel to one field, blocked by a ridge you must dig through. Each later village adds one new element with its own banner: walls (2), gates/rubble (3), stones (4), granite (5), boulders (6), cracks (7), sand (8), hidden pits (9), faults (10). Weak spots: villages 2-4 never require their new tool (opening the spring alone solves them), and a water-supply loss condition exists from village 1.

items.rubric_text: There are no living enemies; the opposition is the terrain and the clock, and the land itself resists the player.
items.comment: There are no creatures. The opposition is granite, rolling boulders, traps and the hunger clock.
items.claude_reason: There are no creatures. The opposition is granite, rolling boulders, traps and the hunger clock.

items.rubric_text: Saving a field makes its crops grow green on the spot, and a saved village carries its clean, unblocked spring forward so the next village has a fuller water supply.
items.comment: A watered field turns green with a burst of particles on the spot. Each saved village adds +8% water supply (capped at +40%) to the next one, and the between screen announces it.
items.claude_reason: A watered field turns green with a burst of particles on the spot. Each saved village adds +8% water supply (capped at +40%) to the next one, and the between screen announces it.

items.rubric_text: Each village sits lower in the hills and grows larger, with more fields, longer routes, and steeper drops, and later villages add boulders, then traps, then traps that interact with the player's own walls.
items.comment: Elevation labels descend from 1,420m to 60m, grids grow from 24x26 to 36x36, fields go from 1 to 4, and slopeDrop rises from 5.2 to 8.6. Boulders arrive at village 6, traps at 7-9 and wall-interacting fault traps at 10, which matches the order the design asks for.

items.rubric_text: A competent first-time player needs at least fifteen minutes to beat the game.
items.comment: There are 12 villages, and all of them are too easy to beat
items.claude_reason: There are 12 villages, but in simulation an informed route saves most of them in 5-40 seconds of water flow, and villages 2-4 save themselves when the spring is opened. The human evaluator called it 'too easy... win with a couple of clicks'. My estimate for a first-time player is about 8-15 minutes, likely under 15.

items.rubric_text: Later parts of the game add at least one new element — a hazard, an enemy, a mechanic or a situation — rather than only more of the same.
items.comment: Later villages add new elements rather than only more of the same: granite that cannot be dug, rolling boulders that crush channels, cracks, thirsty sand, hidden pits that collapse, and fault seams that cave in under walls.
items.claude_reason: Later villages add new elements rather than only more of the same: granite that cannot be dug, rolling boulders that crush channels, cracks, thirsty sand, hidden pits that collapse, and fault seams that cave in under walls.

items.rubric_text: The game gets harder as it goes in at least two different ways, rather than only by making things faster, and stays beatable.
items.comment: Even though the game gets harder, it's still too easy
items.claude_reason: Difficulty rises along several axes: more fields to split water between, larger maps with longer routes, more hazard types per map, and less spare water. A straight-line dig works through village 7 but fails from village 8 on, where routing around hazards is needed. The curve is not monotonic (villages 2-4 are trivial), and my naive route-finder did not clear villages 11-12, so beatability there is unconfirmed.

items.rubric_text: Each mechanic can be tried at least once somewhere safe before the game depends on it.
items.comment: Each mechanic debuts on its own village with a banner telling the player exactly what to do, and restarting is instant, so it can be tried safely. The walls/stones/sluice villages don't force the tool to be used, but the player can still try it there with no penalty.

items.rubric_text: At least one reward changes what the player can do or where they can go, rather than only raising a number.
items.comment: The only carried-over reward is +8% water supply per saved village, which raises a number. Greening fields is cosmetic, all villages are unlocked from the start, and no reward unlocks a new tool, area or ability.

items.rubric_text: Overcoming the opposition takes at least two different player behaviours.
items.comment: Clearing later villages takes at least digging routes around granite and traps plus opening sluice gates or clearing rubble. Damming with stones or walls and nudging boulders are also available.

Damming with stones or walls and nudging boulders are also available. The human evaluator felt little thought was needed, but more than one behaviour is required.

items.rubric_text: Each village has a defined end the player can stop at and come back from.
items.comment: Each village ends in a clear saved or failed state, with Back to Main Menu on the between and fail screens. The menu marks saved villages and Start continues from the first unsaved one. Progress is not saved across reloads (no localStorage), but every village can be selected from the menu at any time.

items.rubric_text: Five minutes of trying to break the game finds nothing visibly wrong — nothing floating, overlapping or drawn in the wrong place, no animation that never settles, no number that disagrees with the screen — and nothing that blocks progress or forces a reload.
items.comment: On villages with 3-4 fields (8-12) the field-status panel moves left and is drawn under the tutorial banner, hiding the first field badges. The cursor label stays on 'Mountain Spring Gate (Click to Open)' after the spring is open until the mouse moves. Sand, hidden-pit and rock shadows render as blurry glowing smears. No console errors and nothing blocked progress.

items.rubric_text: A player given no instructions works out every control and every mechanic from the game alone within the first village.

Mechanics like boulders, pits and faults can't be learned in village 1 because they don't appear there; each is explained by its village's banner instead. Whether that meets 'within the first village' depends on the reviewer's reading.

items.rubric_text: The game has a deliberate 3D visual style, distinct enough to describe in one sentence, held from the first screen to the last.
items.comment: The art style looks too basic and it's not distinct
items.claude_reason: The look is consistent from intro to ending: a flat-shaded low-poly terracotta diorama with blocky cyan water, grey granite blocks and red-roofed box houses, which turns emerald when saved. It is deliberate but very basic (boulders are cubes, decals are blurry), and the human evaluator rated art 2/5.

items.rubric_text: At least every important action produces a visible reaction — particles, a shake, a squash, a flash — timed well and not overdone.
items.comment: The animations are too basic
items.claude_reason: Digging, rock hits, stone drops, gate openings, pit collapses and field saves each spawn coloured particle bursts. Screen shake fires on boulder crushes, fault cave-ins and pit collapses, and the map greens on a save. The effects are modest and the human rated animation 2/5.

items.rubric_text: The game has at least music or ambience, plus sound effects at the key moments.
items.comment: We have music and simple sound effects
items.claude_reason: Web Audio generates a pentatonic plucked music loop, a water-flow ambience that scales with active water, and separate effects for dig, wall, rock hit, stone, boulder, sluice, trap, field drink, village saved and fail. I could not listen in headless mode; the human rated audio 3/5.

items.rubric_text: The interface is understood at a glance, with the most important information standing out and matching the rest of the game visually.
items.comment: The warm timber-styled panels match the game, and hunger and water bars read clearly on 1-2 field villages. On 3-4 field villages the field-status row collides with the tutorial banner and hides field badges, so the key 'which field is dry' information is obscured. The human evaluator rated UI 2/5 and called it 'buggy'.

items.rubric_text: The player can run, jump, and belly-slide down the mountain, dodging hazards and hunting shortcuts to reach the bottom before the clock runs out.

items.rubric_text: On a steep slope the player drops the mother to her belly to slide; sliding builds far more speed than running, but the faster she goes the harder she is to steer.

The blind annotator also confirmed that sliding is clearly faster and harder to control.

items.rubric_text: The mother can at least run, turn, and jump over packed snow and ice; loose snow slows her, while sheer ice keeps her momentum but grips less.

items.rubric_text: A competent first-time player needs at least fifteen minutes to beat the game.
items.comment: There are 8 mountains, but each is a 25-55 second run. A simple scripted bot beat the whole game in about 4.8 minutes of play time (25, 28, 39, 31, 32, 39, 41 and 54 seconds) and still had 64-85 seconds left on every clock. items.rubric_text: Every strike is judged against the beat: a clean hit rows the crew and feeds the score, a weak hit rows them but earns less, and a missed note breaks the rowers' rhythm; consecutive clean hits build a combo multiplier that raises the score each further hit earns, and any miss resets it; a single shared crew cohesion meter refills on clean hits and empties on misses, and at zero the rowers fall out of time and the ship sinks, ending the voyage; forward progress is the score, and reaching the required score before the song ends completes the voyage; a voyage is won by reaching the required score before the song ends and lost by sinking or by letting the song end short of the score.
items.comment: All the required pieces are in the code and were seen in play: Clean/Weak/Miss judgments with Weak paying less (45 against 100), a combo multiplier from 1x to 5x that resets on a miss, one shared cohesion meter that refills on clean hits and drains on misses, sinking at 0, and score shown as voyage progress against a target. A voyage also fails if the song ends short of the target.

In practice, though, a voyage is won about 7-10s into a 2+ minute song, so the build-up within a voyage is barely seen; the roughness rises mainly across voyages (Calm Fjord 20% in Voyage I against Storm Gale 70% in Voyage VIII).

items.comment: The code has escalation built in: BPM goes from 100 to 140, missDrain rises from 11 to 19, cleanRefill falls, and chords, holds, eighth-note streams and surges are added. But the target scores are hit within the first 7-10 seconds of every voyage, mostly while the opening notes are still flagged safe practice (misses there cost nothing). So the denser patterns and harsher cohesion that come later in each song are never reached. 0.0.comment: The game opens on a 3D camera sweep over a sun-baked village-1 farm with the WELLSPRING title and three drought captions, and it can be watched (auto-advances after 15s) or skipped. The main menu has Start/How to Play/Settings and a 12-card village selector.

0.1.comment: Villages load in an angled top-down view with the spring basin bubbling behind its gate at the top and the field plots at the bottom edge. The hunger meter starts draining on load, before any input (134s down to 131s while idle).

0.2.comment: Left-drag digs channels, Shift+drag raises walls, right-click picks up and drops stones, and clicking rubble walls or sluice gates clears or opens them. Digging, walls and stones were driven with real mouse input, and gate/wall clicks were checked in code and simulation.

0.3.comment: Clicking the spring gate (or the Open Spring button) releases the water. It runs down the channel the player carved through the ridge and spills along low ground elsewhere.

0.4.comment: Tools stay usable while the water runs, and cracks, sand, open pits, faults, dry ground and map edges all drain water into a lost-water total that can fail the level. Many villages were solved by routing before opening the spring, so live steering is possible but rarely forced.

0.5.comment: Once water reaches a field along a connected wet path, the field fills, its crops turn green and the badge reads WATERED. The village is saved with hunger time to spare.

0.6.comment: A saved village greens over for about 2 seconds, then a VILLAGE SAVED screen with a valley map leads to the next village. Grids and field counts grow (24x26/1 field up to 36x36/4 fields), but villages 2-4 save themselves when the spring is simply opened, so 'harder' does not hold at every step.

0.7.comment: When hunger empties, a 'Drought Prevails' screen offers Retry and Back to menu, and Retry reloads the village. Saving village 12 plays 'The Watershed Restored' ending, where a green wave sweeps the delta under a blue sky.

1.0.comment: Water is a real heightfield simulation: it flows to lower neighbours, follows dug channels, is blocked by walls, and fields drink only from cells reached by a breadth-first search from the spring. The 'unbroken path' check is lenient: a cell that was once wet keeps counting as connected because wetness never decays.

1.1.comment: It's possible to pick the rocks, but the controls don't work properly on that

1.2.comment: The ground holds cracks, open pits, thirsty sand, hidden pits that collapse after enough water weight, and fault seams. Hunger drains from load and fails the level at zero, fields drink only connected arriving water, and running out of supply below the remaining need triggers a water-loss fail (seen in sims at ~29s).

1.3.comment: Village 1 is a single straight pre-cut channel to one field, blocked by a ridge you must dig through. Each later village adds one new element with its own banner: walls (2), gates/rubble (3), stones (4), granite (5), boulders (6), cracks (7), sand (8), hidden pits (9), faults (10). Weak spots: villages 2-4 never require their new tool (opening the spring alone solves them), and a water-supply loss condition exists from village 1.

1.4.comment: There are no creatures. The opposition is granite, rolling boulders, traps and the hunger clock.

1.5.comment: A watered field turns green with a burst of particles on the spot. Each saved village adds +8% water supply (capped at +40%) to the next one, and the between screen announces it.

1.6.comment: Elevation labels descend from 1,420m to 60m, grids grow from 24x26 to 36x36, fields go from 1 to 4, and slopeDrop rises from 5.2 to 8.6. Boulders arrive at village 6, traps at 7-9 and wall-interacting fault traps at 10, which matches the order the design asks for.

1.7.comment: The HUD shows a hunger meter (seconds and %), a water supply bar, per-field badges with % and Drinking/Dry/WATERED, a NEXT DRAG pill with the cursor's hover label, and the village name and elevation. All five are present, but on 3-4 field villages the field-status panel slides under the tutorial banner and some badges are hidden (see Bugs/UI).

1.8.comment: The between-village screen works: the village greens in-level, then a 'Village Saved' panel shows a valley map with the path to the next village. The How to Play 'stills' are crude canvas rectangles rather than images of each mechanic in use, and fault traps, hidden-pit collapse and wall-dropping have no still. A reviewer could reasonably accept the abstract diagrams as stills.

2.0.comment: There are 12 villages, and all of them are too easy to beat

2.1.comment: Later villages add new elements rather than only more of the same: granite that cannot be dug, rolling boulders that crush channels, cracks, thirsty sand, hidden pits that collapse, and fault seams that cave in under walls.

2.2.comment: Even though the game gets harder, it's still too easy

2.3.comment: Each mechanic debuts on its own village with a banner telling the player exactly what to do, and restarting is instant, so it can be tried safely. The walls/stones/sluice villages don't force the tool to be used, but the player can still try it there with no penalty.

2.4.comment: The only carried-over reward is +8% water supply per saved village, which raises a number. Greening fields is cosmetic, all villages are unlocked from the start, and no reward unlocks a new tool, area or ability.

2.5.comment: Clearing later villages takes at least digging routes around granite and traps plus opening sluice gates or clearing rubble. Damming with stones or walls and nudging boulders are also available.

2.6.comment: Each village ends in a clear saved or failed state, with Back to Main Menu on the between and fail screens. The menu marks saved villages and Start continues from the first unsaved one. Progress is not saved across reloads (no localStorage), but every village can be selected from the menu at any time.

2.7.comment: On villages with 3-4 fields (8-12) the field-status panel moves left and is drawn under the tutorial banner, hiding the first field badges. The cursor label stays on 'Mountain Spring Gate (Click to Open)' after the spring is open until the mouse moves. Sand, hidden-pit and rock shadows render as blurry glowing smears. No console errors and nothing blocked progress.

2.8.comment: From village 1 a permanent HUD line lists every control (dig, Shift-wall, click gate/obstacle, right-click stone/boulder, scroll zoom), and village 1 includes a stone to practise right-click on. Mechanics like boulders, pits and faults can't be learned in village 1 because they don't appear there; each is explained by its village's banner instead. Whether that meets 'within the first village' depends on the reviewer's reading.

3.0.comment: The art style looks too basic and it's not distinct

3.2.comment: We have music and simple sound effects

3.3.comment: The warm timber-styled panels match the game, and hunger and water bars read clearly on 1-2 field villages. On 3-4 field villages the field-status row collides with the tutorial banner and hides field badges, so the key 'which field is dry' information is obscured. The human evaluator rated UI 2/5 and called it 'buggy'.

3.4.comment: The intro is a staged 3D scene: the camera orbits a parched village with drifting dust particles while three captions set up the drought, the springs and the goal. It is more than a title card.

3.5.comment: Saving a village greens the whole map with a fanfare and particles, then shows a green 'VILLAGE SAVED!' panel with the valley map. Failing shows a darkened map with a red 'DROUGHT PREVAILS' panel, so the two are clearly distinct.

3.6.comment: The ending is its own scene under a blue sky: water courses down the delta and a green wave sweeps the valley, with 'The Watershed Restored' text saying the drought is broken. This closes the intro's premise and differs from a single village win. I reached it by forcing village 12 into the saved state.

0.0.comment: The game opens on a titled 3D scene: the mother on the summit, the giant Skua swooping in, and eight chicks sliding away down the slope, with two captions. It can be skipped with a button, Esc or Space, and it moves on by itself after 7 seconds. The main menu offers Start Descent, How to Play and Settings. The storm itself is only heavy fog plus a caption ('A sudden gale...'). There is no snow or wind on screen.

0.1.comment: Pressing Start Descent puts the mother at the top of the track (s=8). The countdown starts falling right away: 1:49.3 shows within half a second of starting Mt 1.

0.2.comment: W/A/S/D runs and steers, Space jumps and Shift belly-slides. Sliding hit 150 km/h, against 76 km/h running. Hazards (crevasses, spurs, slabs, boulders) knock her down, and two ice-cave shortcuts per mountain are entered by steering right. A scripted bot using these inputs reached the bottom of all eight mountains before the clock ran out. Movement is tied to a spline track: she can steer side to side but always moves forward.

0.3.comment: Esc pauses at any point in play and freezes the clock. The pause menu has Resume, Sound ON/OFF, Restart Level and Back to Main Menu. All four buttons are wired up.

0.4.comment: Mountains 3, 6 and 8 have a boss (3, 4 and 5 hit points) in the basin near the bottom. The level cannot be won until its HP reaches 0: the player is looped back through the arena until then. The player damages it by sliding into golden crystals or belly-sliding into it mid-swoop. The bot drove off all three bosses.

0.5.comment: Reaching the bottom plays a 3.1-second win scene. The chick hops toward the mother, the 'Pip Freed!' caption shows, and a victory jingle and chirp play. It is short and simple: the chick moves only about 3 units, and the 'ice cage shatters' in the caption is not shown (the cage just disappears).

0.6.comment: When the clock hits zero, a fail scene shows the chick's ice cradle lifted into the sky by the Skua, with a 'Time Ran Out' caption. Then the fail screen offers Retry Mountain and Back to Main Menu. Retry restarts the same mountain with a full clock.

0.7.comment: After each mountain a story screen shows the mother with her rescued chicks behind her, the flock count, a perk and the next mountain. Steepness rises every time (19% to 35%). The clock does not always get tighter, though. Boss mountains get more time than the mountain before them (Mt 2 104s then Mt 3 118s; Mt 5 102s then Mt 6 118s; Mt 7 105s then Mt 8 126s), and the story screen shows these larger numbers. The bot's leftover time also went up on those mountains. If the reviewer counts the boss fight as using up the extra time, this could pass.

0.8.comment: Each win frees one chick and raises the rescued count. Beating the Apex Storm Raptor on Mt 8 frees Aurora, and the game goes straight to the 'Family Reunited' ending with all eight chicks around the mother. After 11 seconds it returns to the main menu.

1.0.comment: Holding Shift drops her onto her belly. Top slide speed is about 150 km/h on ice, against about 76 km/h running. Steering acceleration is divided by a speed factor that grows about 4x faster while sliding (1.55 vs 0.38), so fast slides turn wide. The blind annotator also confirmed that sliding is clearly faster and harder to control.

1.1.comment: She runs, steers left and right, and jumps. Loose snow on the outer drifts caps speed at 60% and has higher drag. Sheer blue ice has low drag, so it keeps momentum, and grip of 0.58 with slower lateral damping. 'Turn' is only lateral steering on a fixed track: she cannot turn freely or stop (holding S still moves her at about 34 km/h).

1.2.comment: Each mountain has a countdown. Reaching the chick wins and a clock at zero loses. Hazards cause a 1.15-second knockdown and a speed cut but never end the run. Crevasses, ice spurs and falling snow slabs (which drop from above) all exist, plus rolling boulders. The two ice-cave shortcuts per mountain give a 28% distance gain on a 4.3-wide lane with extra hazards inside.

1.3.comment: Mt 1 is wide and nearly straight for its first 42%. It opens with a run/look prompt and a single crevasse with a jump prompt. Next comes a long hazard-free sheer-ice slope with a 'New Move: The Belly Slide' overlay. Hazards begin only at s=405, introduced as spur, then crevasse, then slab, each with its own overlay. Predator swoops are held back until s>560.

1.4.comment: The Skua circles above the player and, on a timer, marks a red ring and swoops. A hit pushes the mother sideways and knocks her down. On timeout it carries off the chick's cradle. On Mt 3, 6 and 8 it blocks the basin as a boss that is driven off by dodging swoops and hitting crystals or ramming it while sliding.

1.5.comment: Fish lines along the route give 100 points each and are counted on the HUD. Orange speed-burst orbs give 4 seconds at up to 41 m/s and ignore loose-snow slowdown. Cyan shield orbs absorb one knockdown. Freeing each chick is the level goal.

1.6.comment: The story screen renders the mother with the rescued chicks lined up behind her, and the count grows each time. Each chick also grants a permanent perk. Later mountains are longer, steeper and narrower, with denser hazards and more frequent swoops. Boulders join from Mt 3, bosses appear on 3/6/8, and the family reunites at the end. Clocks are not consistently tighter: boss mountains get more time.

1.7.comment: The HUD shows the countdown clock, a goal arrow with the distance to the named chick, speed in km/h with stance and surface pills, the fish count and score, and a predator/boss bar. The bar shows swoop warnings, or the boss's integrity as hits remaining.

1.8.comment: How to Play has four cards: the controls, the slide and surfaces, hazards/shortcuts/clock, and predator/bosses/power-ups. The slide key is left off on purpose, as the design doc asks. Between mountains, the story screen shows the growing flock rendered in 3D plus a 'Next Mountain Ahead' card with its clock, steepness and boss warning.

2.0.comment: There are 8 mountains, but each is a 25-55 second run. A simple scripted bot beat the whole game in about 4.8 minutes of play time (25, 28, 39, 31, 32, 39, 41 and 54 seconds) and still had 64-85 seconds left on every clock. With clocks that loose, a first-time player will rarely fail. Even at twice the bot's pace, plus cutscenes and story screens, the game comes out at around 10 minutes, well short of 15.

2.1.comment: Later mountains add rolling frost boulders, which sweep sideways. In code they appear from Mt 3 onward (mtIdx>=2), although the notes say Mt 4. They also add boss arenas with a new crystal-strike or ramming mechanic on Mt 3/6/8, and the lighting shifts from day to dusk to night.

2.2.comment: Difficulty rises in several ways besides speed. The hazard spacing tightens (44 to about 26 m), the track narrows (17.5 to 13.2), swoops come more often (13.5s to 6.8s), boulders are added, and boss HP grows from 3 to 4 to 5. The game stays beatable, since the bot won every mountain. The overall challenge stays low, though, because the clocks leave a large margin throughout.

2.3.comment: Mt 1 lets the player try running, one isolated crevasse jump, and sliding on a long hazard-free ice slope before hazards start. Shortcuts and swoops come later in Mt 1, each with an overlay. Missing the crevasse jump only costs a moment. The boss crystal/ram mechanic has no practice area: it is first explained by an overlay during the Mt 3 boss. Losing there only happens if the clock runs out, which is lenient.

2.4.comment: The shield lets the player take one hit without a knockdown. The speed burst lets her cross loose snow at full speed. The permanent flock perks change her abilities: a free shield at the start of each mountain, higher jumps, faster recovery and better ice grip.

2.5.comment: Getting past the opposition takes steering around the swoop rings and hazards, jumping crevasses and spurs, and sliding into crystals or the boss to damage it. The annotator noted that the boss arena keeps looping the player back, and that this repetition eventually lands hits for them. That weakens how much skill the boss needs.

2.6.comment: Each mountain ends in a win or fail scene, followed by the story or fail screen with Back to Main Menu. Rescued and unlocked counts are saved to localStorage, and the main menu has a mountain grid to pick from. The unlock is never enforced, though: any mountain can be picked from the start.

2.7.comment: There are no console errors, but several visible problems. The HUD's predator/boss bar draws on top of the pause menu panel. In the ice caves the camera clips into the arch geometry, and the shield bubble hides the mother. The boss arena silently teleports the player back up the slope until the boss is beaten. In the intro, the mother stays tinted red and keeps tumbling. The blind annotator also clipped through the blue archways into a lower floor section.

2.8.comment: There is a bug that I'm teletransported to the top of the mountain in loop

3.0.comment: The game has a consistent low-poly which does not pass the quality bar

3.1.comment: The animations are bugged , and sometimes when I'm hit i can go below the floor

3.2.comment: A procedural Web Audio arpeggio loop plays as music, with a calmer variant in menus and a faster tempo when the clock is urgent. Wind or slide noise plays at speed. There are separate sound effects for jump, slide, fish, power-up, knockdown, shield break, screech, boss hit, chirp, victory and fail. Audio could not be heard headless, but the annotator rated it 4/5.

3.3.comment: The UI is built from dark glass cards in a matching icy palette. The clock is large and centred at the top, and speed is large at bottom-left, so the key numbers stand out. The HUD is fairly busy, with five cards and a centre overlay, and the boss bar overlaps the pause panel. The annotator rated UI 4/5.

3.4.comment: The intro is a staged 3D scene, not just a title card. The camera sways over the summit as the Skua swoops past and the eight chicks slide away down the slope while the mother is knocked over, with two captions setting up the premise. The 'storm' itself is only thick fog: no falling snow or wind is shown.

3.5.comment: A win plays a victory jingle and chirp, the chick hops to the mother at the bottom, and a gold 'Pip Freed!' caption shows before the story screen. A loss is clearly different: a descending fail tune and screech, the cradle carried off into the sky, and a red 'Time Ran Out!' screen.

3.6.comment: The ending is its own 'Family Reunited' screen. The camera orbits the mother as all eight chicks circle and hop around her under warmer light. The captions name all eight chicks, show the final score and say the bird of prey is gone, closing the storm and Skua premise from the intro. It is clearly distinct from a single-level win.

0.0.comment: The game opens on the OARSONG title over a 3D scene of the longship at sea, with three captioned camera shots (Next Scene) and a skip button (also Esc/Space), then goes to a main menu with Start Voyage, Voyage Select, How to Play and Settings. The 'launch' is mostly told by the captions ('Cast off the mooring lines!'). The ship just sits on the water while the camera moves; there is no undocking action.

0.1.comment: Start Voyage launches Voyage I. The procedural song starts on the song clock, and rune-block notes ride down four colored deck lanes toward a hit line with D/F/J/K badges.

0.2.comment: Real D/F/J/K key presses timed to the notes registered as CLEAN hits. They raised the score, built the combo (the streak count went up to 2x) and boosted oar power and ship speed.

0.3.comment: Clean hits refill cohesion, cut oarDesync and raise shipSpeed, which makes the cliffs scroll faster. Misses and off-beat strikes (within 330ms of a note) reset the combo, drain cohesion by missDrain, desync the oars and slow the ship. The human annotator said the crew seems to row all the time and the ship moves even on misses: oarStrokePhase always advances and speed only changes within 0.45 to 2.2, so the visual feedback is subtle.

0.4.comment: With no input on Voyage VIII, cohesion fell to 0 after about 7s. The ship visibly heaved down and tipped into the water, then 'The Longship Foundered' appeared with Retry Voyage and Back to Main Menu. Retry restarted the voyage.

0.5.comment: Reaching the target score triggers a horn and the 'VOYAGE COMPLETE!' banner, then a results screen. It shows the score against the required score, max combo, accuracy, the unlocked relic and a 'Next Voyage: Voyage II...' button.

0.6.comment: An in-page autoplayer (calling the game's own handleLaneKeyDown/Up) cleared all 8 voyages in sequence. Finishing Voyage VIII went straight into the 3-shot 'Landfall at High Hall' ending, and clicking through it returned to the main menu.

1.0.comment: There are four lanes over the deck with their own keys (D/F/J/K) and a hit line. On-beat strikes row the crew and push the ship. A strike that is off the beat while a note is near counts as an 'OFF-BEAT!' miss and drains cohesion toward sinking, and tapping with no note nearby is free.

1.1.comment: All the required pieces are in the code and were seen in play: Clean/Weak/Miss judgments with Weak paying less (45 against 100), a combo multiplier from 1x to 5x that resets on a miss, one shared cohesion meter that refills on clean hits and drains on misses, sinking at 0, and score shown as voyage progress against a target. A voyage also fails if the song ends short of the target.

1.2.comment: I was not able to detect visible signs of changes in the ocean

1.3.comment: How to Play covers the lanes, hit line, judgments, cohesion, War Cry and the score target. Voyage I brings in D, F, J and K one at a time with callouts and 'Safe Practice' notes that cost no cohesion, and Voyages II and III open with safe chord and hold practice under a 'NEW MECHANIC' callout. However, scoring counts during practice, so a good player wins Voyage I at about 8s, before lanes J and K have even been introduced.

1.4.comment: There are no enemies. The opposition is the rising sea (pitch, spray, lightning), the song's rising BPM and density, and the cohesion meter. This matches the design, though in practice voyages end before the pressure builds.

1.5.comment: Clean hits pay score times the combo multiplier. Reaching 100% cohesion triggers the War Cry (2x, horn blast, gold banner), which ends on a miss. Completing a voyage unlocks the next one and a relic.

1.6.comment: The code has escalation built in: BPM goes from 100 to 140, missDrain rises from 11 to 19, cleanRefill falls, and chords, holds, eighth-note streams and surges are added. But the target scores are hit within the first 7-10 seconds of every voyage, mostly while the opening notes are still flagged safe practice (misses there cost nothing). So the denser patterns and harsher cohesion that come later in each song are never reached. A perfect player won the voyages at song times of 8.5, 7.8, 8.5, 6.8, 7.4, 6.8, 7.3 and 6.5s, and an 80%-accuracy player won Voyage VIII at 10.1s.

1.7.comment: The HUD shows the lanes with the hit line and key badges, a large timing judgment (CLEAN!/WEAK/MISS with points), the combo multiplier and streak, the cohesion bar with status text, a War Cry banner, a voyage progress bar (score / target) and a 'Sea & Song Intensity' bar with labels.

1.8.comment: Voyage Select ('The Northern Course') shows 8 cards, locked or unlocked, with target and best scores. You select a card and press 'Set Sail on Selected Voyage' (or double-click), and there is a Back to Main Menu button. How to Play explains the lanes, hit line, judgments, cohesion, War Cry, holds and chords.

2.0.comment: The game takes far less than fifteen minutes. The target scores are reached within about 7-10s of song time in every voyage: a perfect autoplayer finished all 8 voyages in about 60s of total play, and an 80%-accuracy player won Voyage VIII at 10s. Even with several retries, a competent first-time player would finish in a few minutes. The 2:00-2:20 song lengths are never used.

2.1.comment: Even though the game add extra challenges they not work properly, for example the hold does not work

2.2.comment: The difficulty levers in the code (faster BPM and note speed, more miss drain, denser charts, rougher sea pitch) would count as several kinds of difficulty, but almost none of it reaches the player. Every voyage ends about 7-10 seconds in, mostly inside the safe-practice opening bars, so later voyages are not meaningfully harder to win. Only the starting sea roughness and BPM are noticeably different.

2.3.comment: Every mechanic gets safe-practice notes with a callout before it can cost cohesion: each lane in Voyage I, chords in Voyage II's first 3 bars and holds in Voyage III's first 3 bars. Misses on those notes only show 'PRACTICE MISS'.

2.4.comment: Completing a voyage unlocks the next one on Voyage Select (somewhere new to go), and each relic changes the rules. For example, Sunstone Compass widens the clean window by 12ms, Dragon Prow raises starting cohesion and Shield-Wall cuts the drain by 20%. The relic effects are real in code but small.

2.5.comment: Within the short span of each voyage, the player has to single-tap notes on beat, strike two lanes together for chords (Voyage II) and hold keys through hold tails (Voyage III).

2.6.comment: Each voyage is one song with a clear end: a results screen or a fail screen. Progress (unlocked voyages and best scores) is kept in Voyage Select for the session. Note that nothing is saved to storage, so a page reload resets progress.

2.7.comment: I found no console errors or blocking bugs, but there are visible problems. The voyage is declared complete about 8s into a song whose HUD says 2:00, while the tutorial callout for lane 2 is still on screen (shot 14). Cohesion can display 100% without the War Cry triggering, because 99.5 is rounded to 100% while the HUD still reads 'Fill to 100% for War Cry (0% left)' (shot 12). The annotator also reported hold-note tails disappearing early.

2.8.comment: On-deck D/F/J/K badges sit under each lane and light up on press. Voyage I's callouts name each key as its lane comes in, and the Voyage II and III callouts explain chords and holds, so the controls are discoverable without the manual. Esc for pause is shown on the HUD Pause button.

3.0.comment: The game has a low poly simple art style

3.1.comment: The animations are not elaborated enough

3.2.comment: The game features sound effects and music, but they are too similar and fail to stand out, despite being central to the experience.

3.3.comment: At 1280x720 the HUD is clear: progress on top, cohesion and sea on the left, combo on the right, a big central judgment, all in the same gold/slate Nordic style. But it is busy, and the human annotator rated UI readability 2 and called it 'unreadable', possibly at a smaller window. A reviewer should check this at their normal window size.

3.4.comment: The intro has three staged 3D camera shots of the longship among the fjord cliffs and towers, with captions setting up the premise: eight crossings to the High Hall, rowing by your drum and keeping cohesion. The staging is camera drift around a static ship rather than a real launch action.

3.5.comment: A win plays a horn blast, shows a large gold 'VOYAGE COMPLETE! Target Score Reached — Landfall Ahead!' and lights bonfires on the watchtowers, then opens a gold 'VOYAGE COMPLETE!' results panel. A loss instead sinks the ship and shows a red 'THE LONGSHIP FOUNDERED' panel.

3.6.comment: Finishing Voyage VIII skips the results and plays a separate 3-shot ending, 'Landfall at High Hall: The Northern Course is Conquered', under a purple dawn sky with a horn. Its captions close the intro's premise (arriving at the High Hall, the saga sung). It reuses the same ship and box scenery, so it is visually modest.

0.0.comment: The game opens on a staged 3D intro at Harbor Courier Depot where Dispatch Chief Mara sets up the courier's first shift over three lines of dialogue (Next and Skip are available). After it, the main menu offers Start Shift, How to Play (Practice Street) and Settings.

0.1.comment: Start Shift puts the bike just behind a green pickup ring at Harbor Courier Depot, with the clock frozen at 70.0s. Riding through the ring shows 'PACKAGE PICKED UP! CLOCK STARTED!' and the clock starts counting down.

0.2.comment: The player rides through a grid city toward the drop-off, guided by an overhead 3D arrow, a HUD compass arrow with distance, and a radar minimap. Each delivery has chaos hazards on the route, announced by a callout banner. The minimap is mirrored left-right relative to the 3D view, which makes it harder to read the route (see Bugs).

0.3.comment: Hazards stall the bike on contact. Holding Shift spends the boost meter for about 1.42x top speed, and boosting also smashes crates. Neon cut-through alleys and jump ramps let the player cut corners or hop over a parade. The clocks are so loose that boosting is rarely needed to buy back time, but the mechanics are all there.

0.4.comment: Reaching the gold beacon in time shows a 'DELIVERY COMPLETE!' banner with confetti and banks points. It then opens the 'DELIVERY BANKED!' tuning screen, where the player picks one of four upgrades.

0.5.comment: New chaos does arrive: deliveries 2 to 6 each debut a hazard, and later ones combine them. The deadline does not tighten, though. Time limits run 70, 68, 68, 66, 62, 72, 68, 76, 64, 74, 66, 72s, while routes get longer (160m at first, up to about 1100m with the detour at the end), and address changes add 26 to 34s. In practice, later deliveries are no tighter than early ones.

0.6.comment: When the clock reaches zero, the game shows 'CLOCK EMPTIED — SHIFT FAILED!' with Retry Delivery and Back to Main Menu. Retry restarts the same delivery with the clock back to full.

0.7.comment: Clearing deliveries 1 to 11 opens the tuning screen and then the next job (12 jobs in all). Clearing job 12 plays the ending scene at Apex Spire Plaza, and after its last line the game returns to the main menu.

1.0.comment: The clock starts only on pickup. Reaching the drop-off before zero completes the job, and hitting zero sends the player to the shift-failed screen.

1.1.comment: Every job runs between two named landmarks (for example Harbor Courier Depot to Sunny Crust Bakery), and both names appear on the HUD job card. Crashing shows 'STALLED! PACKAGE INTACT!', and the package stays on the rack. There is no code path that removes it.

1.2.comment: Two of the three parts are confirmed. Address changes pause the clock (it held at 95.4s for about 1s, 3.5s pause in code) and add 34s. Hitting a hazard stalls the bike with knockback. Shortcut alleys and ramps exist, but on a uniform grid they rarely shorten a route except around a parade, and the human tester said line choices don't matter. A reviewer should judge whether the shortcuts really reward reading the streets.

1.3.comment: The game lands on the intro and then the main menu. Job 1 is a straight 160m run from Depot to Bakery with only three roadside crates, one overhead arrow and a 70s clock, which is very generous: it took about 3.5s.

1.4.comment: There are no enemies, and four chaos kinds exist. Parade floats are stationary blockers: go around them, take an alley, or jump a ramp. Cows and inflatable mascots are moving hazards whose crossings you time. Flooded streets cap speed at 46% unless you boost or have the grip tuning. Customer address changes redirect the route. The flood slowdown worked in testing (speed capped at 27.8 in the water), although the human tester reported no effect, possibly because they had grip or were boosting. Cows and mascots look small and plain at a distance.

1.5.comment: Drifting and near misses (props and hazards) fill the boost meter and send orbs flying into it: in testing, boost went from 10 to 21 during a short drift. After each delivery the player picks one of four tunings (Top Speed, Grip, Boost Capacity, Handling). The tunings change the bike's stats and carry through the rest of the shift.

1.6.comment: Tunings carry forward, hazard counts grow (from 3 crates to 9 hazards on job 12), deliveries 2 to 6 each add a new chaos kind, address changes push faster route reading, and job 12 ends the game. The 'tighter clock' part is missing. Limits stay in a flat 62 to 76s band while routes lengthen, and detours add up to 34s, so later clocks are effectively looser.

1.7.comment: The HUD shows everything listed: the delivery clock with a bar, the 3D and compass route arrows with distance, pickup and drop-off names, the boost meter, speed with tuning tiers, an orange address-change banner showing the new destination and the added seconds, and chaos callout banners. There is also a minimap, but it is mirrored.

1.8.comment: The tuning screen offers four upgrade cards between deliveries, and the player picks one. How to Play drops the player on a closed practice street with checklist drills for accelerate, steer, drift, boost and a practice delivery, plus a sample parade and cow. Flooded streets, mascots and address changes are not practiced there.

2.0.comment: There are 12 deliveries, but each is short. Grid-route lengths total about 5.9km at around 45 m/s, which is roughly 2 to 3 minutes of riding. In testing, the first two jobs took about 3.5s each against clocks near 70s. Even with slow driving, detours and a few retries, a first-time player is unlikely to need 15 minutes. The human tester also said the clocks were very generous.

2.1.comment: We have more things being added but this not generate enough variety on the game , and soon becomes repetitive

2.2.comment: On paper, difficulty rises through more hazards per job, combined chaos types, longer routes and mid-route detours. But the clocks never tighten and leave several times the time a route needs, so failing barely becomes more likely. Hazards are small, point-sized obstacles that are easy to ride around. It stays beatable, but whether it really gets harder needs a human playthrough.

2.3.comment: The practice street safely covers accelerate, steer, drift, boost, near miss, a parade, a cow and a full pickup and drop-off with no clock. Floods, mascots and address changes are not practiced. Each debuts alone in jobs 4 to 6 with a very generous clock and Retry on failure, so in effect they can be tried before the game depends on them.

2.4.comment: Two tunings change what the player can do, not just numbers. Grip (Hydro-Grip Treads) lets the bike cross flooded streets at full speed instead of slowing to 46%. Boost Capacity lets the bike smash crates without boosting. The flood bypass is checked in code only.

2.5.comment: Getting past the opposition calls for different behaviours: steering around or ramp-jumping parades and crates, timing passes across moving cows and mascots, boosting or detouring around floods, and rerouting after an address change.

2.6.comment: Each delivery ends clearly with the completion banner and tuning screen. Picking a tuning saves progress to localStorage, and the main menu then shows 'Continue Shift (Job #N)'.

2.7.comment: Several visible problems turned up. The radar minimap is mirrored left-right compared with the 3D view: +x is drawn on the right while the camera shows it on the left, so the arrow and minimap disagree, and the human tester reported the same. Streetlamps are drawn as solid posts but the bike drives straight through them; the test passed through one with no collision, matching the human report. The practice-street drill panel overlaps the top-left job card. The job card says 'STATUS: AT DEPOT' at non-depot pickups and right after a drop-off. There were no console errors or progress blockers.

2.8.comment: The in-play HUD always shows the control strip (W/S Ride, A/D Steer, Space Drift, Shift Boost, Mouse Look), the boost meter says 'Hold [SHIFT]', and drifting and near misses visibly fling orbs into the meter, so a player can work out the controls in job 1. Address changes, floods and mascots don't appear until jobs 4 to 6. Each is explained by its banner when it appears, but it can't be discovered within the first delivery.

3.0.comment: The art style is simple and not unique

3.1.comment: Animations are not elaborated enough to be seem like a good game

3.2.comment: The game builds all its sound with Web Audio: an engine drone, a looping bass and lead music track that speeds up in play, and sound effects for pickup, drop-off fanfare, boost, near miss, crash, address change and fail. The audio context was running in headless play, but nothing was listened to.

3.3.comment: The HUD is readable and consistent: a large top-centre clock with a bar, a job card at top-left, speed and tunings at bottom-left, boost at bottom-right, and dark rounded panels with yellow accents that match the menus. The mirrored minimap and the overlap on the practice street hurt it a little. The human tester rated UI readability 3/5.

3.4.comment: The intro is a staged 3D scene, not a title card. The camera orbits the courier bike and green pickup beacon at the depot archway while three dialogue lines set up the first shift and the chaos ahead.

3.5.comment: A completed delivery triggers a 1.65s celebration: a gold confetti burst, a three-note fanfare, a 'DELIVERY COMPLETE!' banner with the remaining time, and 'DELIVERY BANKED! +pts'. The tuning screen follows. Failing looks clearly different: a red 'SHIFT FAILED' screen with a falling tone.

3.6.comment: The ending is its own scene, separate from a delivery win. Set at Apex Spire Plaza, the camera sways beside a golden trophy monument with the bike and package while confetti falls. Three lines close the premise ('cleared all 12 deliveries', crowned #1 Express Legend), then the game returns to the menu. The monument reads as a plain yellow block, and its pedestal partly blocks the shot.

0.0.comment: The game opens on a three-slide intro over a 3D bank room with the LONE OFFICER title and premise text, then a main menu with Start Operation, How to Play and Settings. Start loads Room 1 and play begins.

0.1.comment: Each room has a 1.1 second settle period where robbers hold fire and breachers wait, and the radio feed says 'Entering Room N'. After that the officer can move and fire right away. The settle moment is very short and the characters start in place, so there is little to actually watch.

0.2.comment: Every character has a labelled tag (HOSTAGE, ENFORCER, MARKSMAN, BREACHER, ROOM LEADER), and a sightline laser turns red with a 'HOLD FIRE — CIVILIAN IN SIGHTLINE' warning when a civilian is first in line. The player chooses which target to take first. In Room 6, though, a robber fires through a hostage about 1.5s after entry, before the player can do any real weighing.

0.3.comment: The officer moves with WASD, crouches into cover with C/Ctrl and fires aimed shots that neutralize robbers. Pressing E on an off-guard, reloading, flanked or close robber arrests them. A scripted run cleared Rooms 2–4 by crouching at the counter and shooting robbers when they stood up to fire. Arrest was confirmed in the code and by the on-screen prompt, but a full arrest wasn't completed in play.

0.4.comment: Walking up to a hostage and pressing E 'rescues & secures' them. They turn green, get a HOSTAGE SAFE tag, and the hostage counter drops. Hostages are secured where they stand and never guided anywhere, which counts under the 'securing' wording.

0.5.comment: When the room is clear, a ROOM SECURED banner appears, the north exit turns green, and walking onto the exit pad opens a story screen ('Chapter I — First Footstep') with a Breach Next Room button. There is a chapter for each of rooms 1–9.

0.6.comment: A player shot that hits a hostage, or a robber's shot that does, ends the room at once. A red OPERATION FAILED screen appears with Retry Room and Back to Main Menu, and Retry reloads the same room.

0.7.comment: There are 10 rooms in LEVELS, each with its own layout, robbers and hostages, and they advance one by one through the story screens. Rooms 1–4 were played by input. Later rooms were reached via the debug loadLevel hook, so a full run from start to finish wasn't done.

0.8.comment: Clearing Room 10 and stepping on its exit plays a three-slide ending over the vault, with freed hostages and cuffed robbers, ending on 'The Legend of One Officer'. It then returns to the main menu.

1.0.comment: Every shot is a straight ray that stops at the nearest thing it crosses: wall, tall obstacle, hostage, robber or officer. Hostages are never skipped, and robber shots use the same function. Crouched robbers behind low cover soak up frontal shots as cover. That matches the spec, but it may explain the annotator's 'sometimes your shot doesn't hit the robber'.

1.1.comment: The officer has crouch-cover near objects (C/Ctrl), leans (Q left, V right), an 8-round magazine with finite reserve, and a reload (R) that drops the rounds left in the magazine and takes 1.15s. Pressing E arrests off-guard, reloading or flanked robbers. All of it works. The lean-right key is documented wrongly as E, and any robber within 2.35m can be arrested whether or not he is off-guard.

1.3.comment: Room 1 is a small 14x14 room with one robber who never fires (offGuardTimer 999) and one hostage in open space, so it is safe. Later mechanics get a callout banner in the room where they first appear (cover/reload in R2, moving hostage and keycard in R3, breacher in R5, leader in R6). But they are often introduced together and under live fire. Room 2 kills an idle player in about 4s, and Room 6 fails to crossfire 1.5s after entry.

1.4.comment: Enemies behave like the same and we cannot see the diference between them

1.5.comment: Story chapters between rooms build up the officer's legend, from 'never missing a shot' to robbers 'begging to surrender'. Each arrest gives +4 spare rounds, and gold keycards unlock amber Vantage Doors. There is no score.

1.6.comment: Rooms grow from 14x14 to 26x24, robbers go from 1 to 6, hostages from 1 to 5, and more hostages move in later rooms. Leaders coordinate the crew from Room 6 on, and Rooms 7–9 have tighter ammo. The story keeps building the officer's reputation.

1.7.comment: The HUD shows magazine and reserve ammo, hostages left, robbers loose, an arrested (cuffed) count plus [CUFFED] world tags, a blinking low-ammo/empty warning, and one 'Current Directive' objective line that changes with the situation.

1.8.comment: How to Play has four panels: movement and aiming, the Judgement Shot and fail rule, cover/lean/reload, and arrest vs neutralize plus rescue. That covers everything the item asks for. It lists the lean keys as Q/E, but E is interact and the real right-lean key is V, and Esc for pause isn't listed.

2.0.comment: There are 10 rooms, but each is small: 1 to 6 robbers, and a scripted run cleared Rooms 2–4 in a few seconds each with 2–3 shots. A human will be slower and will retry often, since idle officers die in about 4s and crossfire fails are common. My estimate is roughly 10–15 minutes including story screens, which is borderline. Reviewer should judge from a real playthrough.

2.2.comment: All levels are easy to beat

2.3.comment: In Room 1 the robber never fires, so moving, crouching, shooting, reloading, arresting and rescuing can all be tried safely. Keycards and doors first show up in Room 3 under fire, but they are optional, so the game never depends on them. Enemy types arrive in live rooms with a banner warning.

2.4.comment: Picking up a keycard lets the officer unlock an amber Vantage Door, opening a passage and sightline through an interior wall that was closed. That changes where the player can go. Arrests also give +4 rounds, which lets the player keep firing. The doors are shortcuts, since the walls can also be walked around.

2.5.comment: Winning takes different behaviours. The player shoots exposed robbers, times shots for when crouched Marksmen stand up (they shrug off frontal fire while down), arrests reloading or off-guard robbers up close, repositions against rushers, and goes for the leader first. Just firing at a crouched marksman does nothing.

2.6.comment: Each room has a clear end (ROOM SECURED, exit, story screen). But there is no save, continue or room select: Start Operation always loads Room 1, and nothing persists after a reload or a return to the menu. A player who stops can't come back to the room they reached.

2.7.comment: Room 6 fails on its own 1.5s after entry in 4 of 4 idle trials: the leader fires at the officer through the centre hostage before the player has acted. Robbers are coded to fire even when a hostage is first in line. Lean keys are shown as Q/E while E is interact (lean right is V). In larger rooms the top HUD bar covers the far wall, and tags are cut off under it. The intro/ending text says 32 hostages but the rooms hold 31, and the annotator saw cover stance get stuck.

2.8.comment: The Room 1 banner and context prompts teach WASD, Shift, C/Ctrl, click to fire, E to arrest/rescue, and R through the ammo warning. Lean right (V) is never shown anywhere; the game says E, which does interact instead. Esc to pause isn't shown in play. The key cover rule, that crouched marksmen can't be hit from the front and must be caught standing or disoriented, is never explained.

3.0.comment: No, the art style is simple and boring

3.1.comment: The animations are simple and it's not a game highlight

3.2.comment: There is no music, only some simple sound effects

3.3.comment: The HUD is a consistent navy-and-brass tactical style with large ammo and counters. Coloured world tags make threats and civilians easy to tell apart, and the red HOLD FIRE warning stands out. In bigger rooms the top HUD band covers the back of the room and clips tags; the annotator rated UI 4/5.

3.4.comment: The intro sets up the premise (an armed syndicate seized the bank, backup is twenty minutes out, the officer goes in alone) over three slides. The camera moves around a 3D room with a hostage and a robber. The staging is the Room 1 layout with static characters, so it is light but more than a title card.

3.5.comment: Clearing a room plays a four-note chime and shows a green ROOM SECURED banner, then turns the exit door and floor pad green before the gold story screen. The red fail screen and descending tones are clearly different.

3.6.comment: The ending is its own three-slide cutscene over the Grand Vault, showing every hostage freed in green and every robber cuffed, with the camera moving. It ends with 'The Legend of One Officer', which closes the intro's lone-officer premise. It is clearly different from the per-room banner and story screen.
